title: Hodgkin lymphoma
description: Type of blood and immune-system cancer
wiki_lead:
Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) is a cancer where multinucleated Reed–Sternberg cells (RS cells) are present in the lymph nodes. As it affects a subgroup of white blood cells called lymphocytes, it is a lymphoma. The condition was named after the English physician Thomas Hodgkin, who first described it in 1832. Symptoms may include fever, night sweats, and weight loss. Often, non-painful enlarged lymph nodes occur in the neck, under the arm, or in the groin. People affected may feel tired or be itchy.
The two major types of Hodgkin lymphoma are classic Hodgkin lymphoma and nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma. About half of Hodgkin lymphoma cases arise from Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), and these are generally the classic form. Other risk factors include a family history of the condition and having HIV/AIDS. Diagnosis is conducted by confirming the presence of cancer and identifying Reed–Sternberg cells in lymph node biopsies. The virus-positive cases are classified as a form of the Epstein–Barr virus-associated lymphoproliferative diseases.
Hodgkin lymphoma may be treated with chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and stem-cell transplantation. The choice of treatment often depends on how advanced the cancer has become and whether or not it has favorable features. If the disease is detected early, a cure is often possible. In the United States, 89% of people diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma survive for five years or longer. For those under the age of 20, rates of survival are 97%. Radiation and some chemotherapy drugs, however, increase the risk of other cancers, heart disease, or lung disease over the subsequent decades.
In 2015, about 574,000 people globally had Hodgkin lymphoma, and 23,900 (4.2%) died. In the United States, 0.2% of people are affected at some point in their life. Most people are diagnosed with the disease between the ages of 20 and 34.

Signs and symptoms
People with Hodgkin lymphoma may present with these symptoms:

Lymphadenopathy: The most common symptom of Hodgkin lymphoma is the painless enlargement of one or more lymph nodes. The nodes may also feel rubbery and swollen when examined. The nodes of the neck, armpits and groin (cervical and supraclavicular) are most frequently involved (80–90% of the time, on average). The lymph nodes of the chest are often affected, and these may be noticed on a chest radiograph.
Systemic symptoms: About one-third of people with Hodgkin lymphoma may also present with systemic symptoms, including:
Itchy skin
Night sweats
Unexplained weight loss of at least 10% of the person's total body mass in six months or less
Low-grade fever
Fatigue (lassitude)
Systemic symptoms such as fever, night sweats, and weight loss are known as B symptoms; thus, presence of these indicate that the person's stage is, for example, 2B instead of 2A.

grok_lead: Hodgkin lymphoma is a cancer of the lymphatic system, a network of vessels and glands that is part of the body's immune system and helps remove excess fluids, waste products, and other toxins, characterized by the presence of large, abnormal cells known as Reed-Sternberg cells. First described in 1832 by English physician Thomas Hodgkin based on autopsy findings of seven patients with painless enlargement of lymph nodes and spleen, the disease was later named "Hodgkin's disease" in 1865 by Samuel Wilks to honor his contributions. These Reed-Sternberg cells, identified in 1898 by Carl Sternberg and independently in 1902 by Dorothy Reed, are derived from B lymphocytes and are a hallmark for diagnosis, distinguishing it from non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The disease primarily affects lymph nodes but can spread to the spleen, liver, bone marrow, or other organs, with two main types: classic Hodgkin lymphoma, which accounts for about 95% of cases and includes four subtypes (nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, and lymphocyte-depleted), and nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, a rarer, slower-growing form. Common symptoms include painless swelling of lymph nodes in the neck, armpits, or groin; persistent fatigue; unexplained fever; night sweats; unintentional weight loss; and itchy skin, often prompting medical evaluation. Risk factors include younger age (peak incidence in 20s and 30s or over 65), male sex, family history of lymphoma, prior Epstein-Barr virus infection, HIV, and weakened immune systems, though the exact cause involves genetic mutations in B cells leading to uncontrolled growth. In the United States, approximately 8,720 new cases are estimated for 2025, representing about 0.4% of all cancers, with a lifetime risk of 0.2%; incidence rates are 2.5 per 100,000 people annually, and it is more common in males and certain racial groups. Diagnosis typically involves physical exams, imaging (such as PET-CT scans), blood tests, and lymph node biopsy to confirm Reed-Sternberg cells, followed by staging from I (limited to one lymph node area) to IV (widespread involvement). Treatment has advanced significantly since the mid-20th century, with combination chemotherapy (e.g., ABVD regimen), radiation therapy, targeted therapies like brentuximab vedotin, and immunotherapy offering cure rates up to 90% for early-stage disease; the 5-year relative survival rate is 89%. Despite high curability, long-term survivors may face risks of secondary cancers or cardiovascular issues from prior treatments. In the antiretroviral therapy (ART) era, HIV-positive Hodgkin lymphoma survivors have an elevated risk of second primary cancers, including lung cancer, with second malignancies occurring earlier (often within 5 years, highest risk in the first 2 years) and an approximately 39% higher overall risk compared to HIV-negative survivors. This underscores the importance of ongoing monitoring.
